label: structure-zd
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{structure-zd}  Let $d \geq 1$, and suppose that $F \oplus A = \mathbb{Z}^d$ for some finite set $F \subset \mathbb{Z}^d$ and some $A \subset \mathbb{Z}^d$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] (Dilation lemma) One has $rF \oplus A = \mathbb{Z}^d$ whenever $r$ is a natural number coprime to all primes less than or equal to the cardinality $|F|$ of $F$.
    \item[(ii)] (Structure theorem) If we normalize $0 \in F$, then we have a decomposition
    $$ {\bf 1}_A = {\bf 1}_{\mathbb{Z}^d} - \sum_{f \in F \backslash \{0\}} \varphi_f$$
    where ${\bf 1}_A$ denotes the indicator function of $A$ (thus ${\bf 1}_A(x)=1$ when $x \in A$ and ${\bf 1}_A(x)=0$ otherwise), and for each $f \in F \backslash \{0\}$, $\varphi_f \colon \mathbb{Z}^d \to [0,1]$ is a function which is $qf$-periodic (i.e., $\varphi_f(qf+ x)=\varphi_f(x)$ for every $x\in\mathbb{Z}^d$), where $q$ is the product of all the primes less than or equal to $2|F|$. 
\end{itemize}

label: def:factor
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:factor}  Let $G = (G,+)$ be a group.  For each element $x$ of $G$, let $\lambda(x)$ be an iid element of the unit interval $[0,1]$, thus the $(\lambda(x))_{x \in G}$ are jointly independent random variables, each drawn uniformly at random from $[0,1]$.  A random subset $A$ of $G$ is said to be a \emph{factor of iid process} if there exists a Borel measurable function $\Phi \colon [0,1]^G \to \{0,1\}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{process-eq} {\bf 1}_A(x_0) = \Phi\left( (\lambda(x_0+x))_{x \in G} \right)
\end{equation}
almost surely for all $x_0 \in G$. (In particular, $A$ is a stationary process.)  More generally, a finite collection $A_1,\dots,A_k$ of random subsets of $G$ is a \emph{(joint) factor of iid process} if there exist Borel measurable functions $\Phi_1,\dots,\Phi_k \colon [0,1]^G \to \{0,1\}$ such that
$$
{\bf 1}_{A_i}(x_0) = \Phi_i\left( (\lambda(x_0+x))_{x \in G} \right)
$$
almost surely for all $x_0 \in G$. 

If $F_1,\dots,F_k$ are finite subsets of $G$, a \emph{factor of iid tiling} of $G$ by $F_1,\dots,F_k$ is a joint factor of iid process $A_1,\dots,A_k$ such that
$$ (F_1 \oplus A_1) \uplus \dots \uplus (F_k \oplus A_k) = G$$
almost surely.
head: environment
name: Factor of iid

label: 23-tile
title: Example
body_md:
\label{23-tile}  We can generate a factor of iid tiling of the integers $\mathbb{Z}$ by the tiles $F_1 \coloneqq \{0,1\}$, $F_2 \coloneqq \{0,1,2\}$ by performing the following procedure.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)]  First we generate jointly independent random variables $\lambda(x) \in [0,1]$ for all $x \in \mathbb{Z}$.
    \item[(ii)]  We construct the factor of iid process
    $$ S \coloneqq \{ x \in \mathbb{Z}: \lambda(x) < \lambda(x-1),\lambda(x+1) \}$$
    of ``local minima'' of $\lambda$.  We enumerate $S=\{s_n\colon n\in \mathbb{Z}\}$ by order (i.e., $s_n<s_m$ if $n<m$). Note that $S$ is almost surely unbounded both above and below, and is $2$-separated, in the sense that $s_{n+1} - s_n \geq 2$ for any two consecutive elements $s_n, s_{n+1}$ of $S$.
    \item[(iii)]  Using the process $S=\{s_n\colon n\in \mathbb{Z}\}$, we construct the factor of iid process $S'$ by 
    $$S'\coloneqq \{s_n+2j\in \mathbb{Z} \colon n,j\in\mathbb{Z}, s_n\le s_n+2j\le s_{n+1}-2\}.$$
    We enumerate $S'=\{s'_n\colon n\in \mathbb{Z}\}$ by order.
      Note that $S'$ is also almost surely unbounded above and below, and one has $2 \leq s'_{n+1}-s'_n \leq 3$ for any consecutive elements $s'_n, s'_{n+1}$ of $S'$. 
    \item[(iv)]  Using the process $S'=\{s'_n\colon n\in \mathbb{Z}\}$, we construct the joint factor of iid process $A_1, A_2$ by setting $A_1$ to consist of those elements $s'_n$ of $S'$ for which $s'_{n+1}-s'_n = 2$, and $A_2$ to consist of those elements of $s'_n$ of $S'$ for which $s'_{n+1}-s'_n = 3$.
\end{itemize}
One then easily verifies that $A_1, A_2$ is a factor of iid tiling of $\mathbb{Z}$ by $F_1,F_2$.

On the other hand, there is no factor of iid tiling $F_1 \oplus A_1 = \mathbb{Z}$ of the integers $\mathbb{Z}$ just by $F_1 = \{0,1\}$, due to the ``rigid'' nature of this tiling equation.  Indeed, the only possible values of $A_1$ are the even integers $2\mathbb{Z}$ or the odd integers $2\mathbb{Z}+1$.  The events $0 \in A_1$, $1 \in A_1$ then complement each other and thus must each occur with probability $1/2$ by stationarity.  On the other hand, for any integer $N$, we have $0 \in A_1$ if and only if $2N \in A_1$; sending $N \to \infty$ we conclude that $0 \in A_1$ is a tail event, contradicting the Kolmogorov zero-one law.  A similar argument shows that there is no factor of iid tiling that involves only the tile $F_2 = \{0,1,2\}$.

title: Remark
body_md:
After the submission of the paper, Tim Austin suggested a simpler proof of a stronger version of \cref{thm:tile-factor} saying that \emph{(i)} and \emph{(ii)} in the theorem are equivalent to the third statement:

 \emph{(iii)} Let $A$ be the stationary point process  on $G$ such that $F\oplus A=G$. If $A$ is not trivial then $A$ has positive topological entropy.

The direction ``\emph{(ii)} implies \emph{(iii)}'' is similar to our proof of ``\emph{(ii)} implies \emph{(i)}'' in \cref{sec:factor}. The direction ``\emph{(iii)} implies \emph{(ii)}'' is an immediate corollary of \cref{structure-gen}, but can also be deduced by a more elementary argument similar to the proof of \cite[Lemma 2.15]{cyr-kra}.

label: thm:torus
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:torus}  Let $d \geq 1$, and suppose that we have a measurable tiling $F \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^d$ of the $d$-torus by some finite subset $F = \{f_1,\dots,f_n\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ and some measurable subset $A$ of $\mathbb{T}^d$.  Then there exists a rational tiling $F^0 \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^d$ of the $d$-torus by some finite subset $F^0 = \{f_1^0,\dots,f_n^0\}$ of $\mathbb{Q}^d$, obeying the following additional properties:
\begin{itemize}
    \item [(i)]  If we define the velocities $v_i \coloneqq f_i - f_i^0$ for $i=1,\dots,n$ and the sets $F^t = \{ f_1^0 + tv_1, \dots, f_n^0 + tv_n \}$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$, then we have $F^t \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^d$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$.  In particular, one can continuously (and linearly) deform the original tile set $F = F^1$ to the rational tile set $F^0$ while retaining the measurable tiling property throughout.
    \item[(ii)]  If $d=2$ and we impose the normalization $0 \in F$, then all the velocities $v_i$ are scalar multiples $v_i = \alpha_i v$ of a single  vector $v \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ for some real numbers $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$.  Furthermore, we can partition $F$ into subsets $F_1,\dots,F_k$ such that for each $1 \leq j \leq k$, the elements of $F_j$ have the same velocity (thus $\alpha_i = \alpha_{i'}$ whenever $f_i,f_{i'} \in F_j$), and the set $F_j \oplus A \coloneqq \{ f_i + a: f_i \in F_j, a \in A \}$ is $\mathbb{R} v$-invariant in the sense that $tv + F_j \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} F_j \oplus A$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$.
    \item[(iii)]  If the hypotheses are as in (ii), and furthermore the tile $A$ is open and connected, then we can furthermore assume that either all the velocities $v_i$ vanish (so in particular $F=F^0$ is rational), or else for each $1 \leq j \leq m$, the set $F_j \hbox{ mod } \mathbb{Z}^2$ lies in a coset of $\mathbb{R} v \hbox{ mod } \mathbb{Z}^2$, and all the $F_j$ have the same cardinality.
    \item[(iv)]  If $d=1$, then $F$ is rational; in other words, we have $F = F^0 + v$ for some $v \in \mathbb{R}$.
\end{itemize}

name: Measurable tilings of a torus

title: Example
body_md: Let $d=1$ and $A \coloneqq [0,1/2] \hbox{ mod } \mathbb{Z}$.  Then a measurable tiling $F \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}$ of $A$ necessarily takes the form $F = \{ v, m+1/2+v\}$ for some real number $v$ and integer $m$.  If we then take $F^0 \coloneqq \{ 0, m+1/2\}$, we see that $F = F^0 + v$ is a translate of the  set $F^0 \subset \mathbb{Q}$, thus rational, and that the other translates $F^t = F^0 + tv$ also give a measurable rational tiling: $F^t \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}$.

name: Two dimensions, disconnected

title: Example
body_md:
Let $d=2$ and $A \coloneqq (0,1/2)^2 \hbox{ mod } \mathbb{Z}^2$; this is an open connected set.  Let $\alpha$ be an irrational number.  Then the set
$$ F \coloneqq \{ (0,0), (0+1/2,0), (\alpha,1/2), (\alpha+1/2,1/2)\}$$
generates a measurable tiling $F \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^2$ of the torus $\mathbb{T}^2$.  If for every real $t$ we set
$$ F^t = \{ (0,0), (1/2,0), (t,1/2), (t+1/2,1/2)\}$$
then $F^t \oplus A = _{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^2$ is a measurable tiling for every real number $t$, which is rational when $t=0$.  Also, if we set $v_0 = (1,0)$, and partition $F = F^1$ into
$$ F_1 = \{ (0,0), (1/2,0)\}; \quad F_2 = \{(\alpha,1/2), (\alpha+1/2,1/2)\}\},$$
then we can give the elements of $F_1$ a zero velocity, and the elements of $F_2$ a velocity of $\alpha v_0$, and the sets 
$$ F_1 \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T} \times (0,1/2) ; \quad
F_2 \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}}  \mathbb{T} \times (1/2,1)$$
are $\mathbb{R} v_0$-invariant; informally, this means that one can independently ``slide'' the sets $F_1, F_2$ along the direction $v_0$ without destroying the measurable tiling property. Note that $F_1 \hbox{ mod } \mathbb{Z}^2$ and $F_2 \hbox{ mod } \mathbb{Z}^2$ both lie on cosets of $\mathbb{R} v_0 \hbox{ mod } \mathbb{Z}^2$.

A more complicated example of a connected tile in two dimensions is depicted on the right-hand side in \cref{fig:two_examples}.

label: three-dim
title: Example
body_md:
\label{three-dim}  Let $d=3$ and $A \coloneqq [0,1/2]^3 \hbox{ mod } \mathbb{Z}^3$.  Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be irrational numbers.  For every real number $t$, set
\begin{align*}
     F^t \coloneqq \{ 
     &(0, t\alpha, 0), (0, t\alpha+1/2, 0),\\
     &(1/2, 0, t\beta), (1/2, 0, t\beta+1/2),\\
     &(t\gamma, 1/2, 1/2), (t\gamma+1/2, 1/2, 1/2),\\
     &(0, 0, 1/2), (1/2, 1/2, 0)\}.
\end{align*}One can then verify that $F^t \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^3$ for all real $t$ (see, \cref{fig:cube}).  In particular, one can ``slide'' the irrational tiling $F = F^1$ into the rational tiling $F^0$ without destroying the tiling property, with the elements of $F$ being given velocities proportional to $(1,0,0), (0, 1, 0)$ and $(0,0,1)$, respectively.

body_md: \label{grf}  As showed in  \cite[Lemma~3.1]{GreenfeldTao}, one can generalize the dilation lemma by requiring the tiling to be a \emph{periodic level  tiling} rather than a partition up to null sets, by which we mean that  for every $1\le k\le |F|$, the level set $\{x\colon {\bf 1}_F*{\bf 1}_A(x)=k\}$ is \emph{periodic} in $X$ up to $\mu$-null sets, (where here a periodic  set is a set which is $\mu$-almost everywhere invariant with respect to an action of some  lattice).  The conclusion is then that there is a number $q$ (depending on $F$ and ${\bf 1}_F*{\bf 1}_A$) such that if  $r=1\mod q$ then ${\bf 1}_{F^r}*{\bf 1}_A=_{\mathrm{a.e.}} {\bf 1}_{F}*{\bf 1}_A$,  but now we permit collisions $f_1^r = f_2^r$ to occur.  We leave the details of this generalization to the interested reader.

body_md: \label{quasi-rem}   \cref{structure-gen}(i) easily extends  to the setting in which the action of $\Gamma$ is quasi-invariant rather than invariant, which means that it maps $\mu$-null sets to $\mu$-null sets.  This can be accomplished simply by replacing $\mu$ with the (non-$\sigma$-finite) measure $\tilde \mu$ defined by setting $\tilde \mu(E)$ to equal $+\infty$ when $\mu(E)>0$ and to equal zero otherwise.

body_md: \label{grf2} Using \cref{grf}, one can also extend the above structure theorem to periodic level tilings, and in particular, to \emph{level $k$ tilings}\footnote{Higher level tilings are studied in several places in the literature; see for instance \cite{kol}, \cite{gkrs}, \cite{swee-hong}.}  (by which we mean that almost every element of $X$ lies in precisely $k$ of the translates $f\cdot A$ for some $k\le |F|$), but now replacing ${\bf 1}_X$ in \eqref{onex} with $k {\bf 1}_X$.  However this identity \eqref{onex} is significantly less useful in the $k>1$ case due to the gap in values between $k {\bf 1}_X$ and ${\bf 1}_A$, which leaves more room for the functions $\varphi_f, f\in F$ to vary (cf., \cite[Theorem~1.3(ii)]{GreenfeldTao}).

label: init
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{init}  Let $F \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^d$ be a measurable tiling of a torus $\mathbb{T}^d$ by a finite set $F \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and a measurable set $A \subset \mathbb{T}^d$. We normalize $0 \in F$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)]  (Weak rationality) For every $f \in F$, there exists $k \in \mathbb{Z}^d \backslash \{0\}$ such that $k \cdot f \in \mathbb{Z}$.
    \item[(ii)]  (Weak structure)  Up to sets of measure zero, one can write
    $$ \bigcup_{f \in F \cap \mathbb{Q}^d} (f + A) = \bigcap_{f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^d} A_f$$
    where for each $f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^d$, $A_f$ is a $qf$-invariant measurable subset of $\mathbb{T}^d$ for some natural number $q$ with $0 < \mu(A_f) < 1$.
\end{itemize}
head: environment
name: Initial properties

title: Proof
body_md:
We begin with (i).  From \cref{structure-gen}(ii) we have a decomposition
$$ {\bf 1}_{\mathbb{T}^d} = {\bf 1}_A + \sum_{f \in F \backslash \{0\}} \varphi_f$$
where for each $f \in F \backslash \{0\}$,  $\varphi_f \colon \mathbb{T}^d \to [0,1]$ is a measurable function of mean $\mu(A) = 1/|F|$ which is $qf$-invariant for some natural number $q$.  Now if $f \in F \backslash \{0\}$ is such that $k \cdot f \not \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $k \in \mathbb{Z}^d \backslash \{0\}$, then by the Weyl equidistribution theorem, the action of $qf$ is ergodic, thus $\varphi_f$ is almost everywhere equal to a constant, which must be $1/|F|$.  Thus in this case we have the inequality
$$ {\bf 1}_{\mathbb{T}^d} \geq {\bf 1}_A + \frac{1}{|F|}$$
almost everywhere, which is a contradiction since $A$ has positive measure.  This proves (i).

Now we prove (ii).  Let $\tilde q$ be a natural number divisible by all primes less than or equal to $|F|$ such that $\tilde qf = 0 \hbox{ mod } \mathbb{Z}^d$ for all $f \in F \cap \mathbb{Q}^d$.  From \cref{structure-gen}(ii) we have
\begin{equation}\label{con}
 {\bf 1}_{\mathbb{T}^d} = \sum_{f \in F \cap \mathbb{Q}^d} {\bf 1}_{f + A} + \sum_{f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^d} \tilde \varphi_f
 \end{equation}
 where for each $f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^d$,  $\tilde \varphi_f \colon \mathbb{T}^d \to [0,1]$ is a measurable function which is $\tilde qf$-invariant and has positive mean.  If we let $A_f$ denote the complement of the support of $\tilde \varphi_f$, then $A_f$ is also $\tilde qf$-invariant and has measure less than $1$.  Note that, up to sets of measure zero, $\sum_{f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^d} \tilde \varphi_f$ vanishes precisely on $\bigcap_{f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^d} A_f$, and $\sum_{f \in F \cap \mathbb{Q}^d} {\bf 1}_{f + A}$ is the indicator function of $\bigcup_{f \in F \cap \mathbb{Q}^d} f+A$.  The claim (ii) then follows from \eqref{con} (note that none of the $A_f$ can have zero measure since $\bigcup_{f \in F \cap \mathbb{Q}^d} (f + A)$ has positive measure).

title: Remark
body_md:
Using \cref{thm:torus}(iv), it is possible to fully describe all measurable tilings of the circle in terms of tilings of finite cyclic groups.
Namely, given $F=\{f_1,\dots, f_n\}\subseteq \mathbb{Q}$ and assuming that $f_1=0$, we find a $g\in \mathbb{T}^1\cap \mathbb{Q}$ such that $\langle g\rangle$, the cyclic group generated by $g$, contains $F'=\{f_1\mod 1,\dots, f_n\mod 1\}$ and is minimal with respect to set inclusion; for instance one can take $g = \frac{1}{q} \mod 1$ where $q$ is the least common multiple of the denominators of elements from $F$.
Let $\mathcal{T}_{g,F'}$ be the set of all $A'\subseteq \langle g\rangle$ such that $F'\oplus A'=\langle g\rangle$, i.e., $\mathcal{T}_{g,F'}$ consists of all tiles of the finite cyclic group $\langle g\rangle$ using translates $F'$.
Consider the action of $\langle g\rangle$ on $\mathbb{T}^1$ induced by $x\mapsto g+x$.
As $g\in \mathbb{Q}$, we infer that orbit of each $x\in \mathbb{T}^1$ is finite, in fact, of cardinality $|\langle g\rangle|$.
It follows that there is a measurable set $X\subseteq \mathbb{T}^1$ that intersects each orbit of the $\langle g\rangle$ in exactly one point.

There is a one-to-one correspondence between measurable sets $A\subseteq \mathbb{T}^1$ that satisfies $F\oplus A=_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^1$ and measurable functions
$$\psi:X\to \mathcal{T}_{g,F},$$
(where $\mathcal{T}_{g,F}$ is endowed with the discrete $\sigma$-algebra) that is given as follows: the measurable set $A_\psi$, that corresponds to $\psi$, is defined as $$A_\psi=\left\{y\in \mathbb{T}^1:\exists x\in X \ y\in \psi(x)+x\right \}.$$
Similarly, given a measurable tile $A$, the function
$$\psi_A(x)=\{h\in \langle g\rangle:h+x\in A\},$$
defined for $x\in X$, is measurable and $\psi_A(x)\in \mathcal{T}_{g,F'}$ almost surely.

label: parallel
title: Proposition
body_md: \label{parallel}  For any $f_1, f_2 \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^2$, one has $h_{f_1} = \pm h_{f_2}$.
head: environment
name: All shifts are parallel

label: onet2
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $q$ be a natural number divisible by all the primes up to $|F|$, such that $qf \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ for all $f \in F\cap \mathbb{Q}^2$.  By \cref{structure-gen}(ii), we have a decomposition
\begin{equation}\label{onet2}
 {\bf 1}_{\mathbb{T}^2} =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \sum_{f \in F \cap \mathbb{Q}^2} {\bf 1}_{f+A} + \sum_{f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^2} \varphi_f
 \end{equation}
 where for each $f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^2$, $\varphi_f \colon \mathbb{T}^2 \to [0,1]$ is $qf$-invariant and has mean $\mu(A)=1/|F|$.

For each $f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^2$, some integer multiple $kqf$ of $f$ lies in the subtorus
$$ \langle h_f \rangle^\perp \coloneqq \{ x \in \mathbb{T}^2: h_f \cdot x = 0 \}.$$
Since $f \not \in \mathbb{Q}^2$, the translation action of $kqf$ is ergodic on this subtorus.  We conclude that $\varphi_f$ is in fact $\langle h_f \rangle^\perp$-invariant.  If we then define
$$ \Phi_1 \coloneqq \sum_{f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^2: h_f = \pm h_{f_1}} \varphi_f$$
then $\Phi_1$ is also $\langle h_{f_1} \rangle^\perp$-invariant.  On reducing \eqref{onet2} modulo one, we have
\begin{equation}\label{ont}
0 =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \Phi_1 + \sum_{f \in F_1} \varphi_f \hbox{ mod } 1,
\end{equation}
where $F_1$ consists of those $f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^2$ with $h_f \neq \pm h_{f_1}$.
To eliminate the $\varphi_f$ terms we introduce the difference operators
$$ \partial_v g(x) \coloneqq g(x) - g(x-v)$$
for any $g \colon \mathbb{T}^2 \to \mathbb{T}$ and $v \in \mathbb{T}^2$.  Observe that these operators $\partial_v$ commute with each other.  If $f \in F_1$  we have
$$ \langle h_f \rangle^\perp + \langle h_{f_1} \rangle^\perp = \mathbb{T}^2$$
and hence if $g_f \in \mathbb{T}^2$  we may decompose $g_f = g'_f + g''_f$ where $g'_f \in \langle h_f \rangle^\perp$ and $g''_f \in \langle h_{f_1} \rangle^\perp$.  We then obtain the identities
$$ \partial_{g'_f} \Phi_1 =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \partial_{g_f} \Phi_{1}$$
and
$$ \partial_{g'_f} \varphi_f =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} 0.$$
If one then applies each of the operators $\partial_{g'_f}$ in turn to \eqref{ont} for $f \in F_1$ to eliminate the $\varphi_f$ terms, we conclude that
$$ \left(\prod_{f \in F_1} \partial_{g_f}\right) \Phi_{1} =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} 0 \hbox{ mod } 1$$
whenever $g_f \in \mathbb{T}^2$.  Since $\Phi_{1}$ is $\langle h_{f_1} \rangle^\perp$-invariant, we may write
$$ \Phi_{1}(x) =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \tilde \Phi_1(h_{f_1} \cdot x) \hbox{ mod } 1$$
for some measurable function $\tilde \Phi_1 \colon \mathbb{T} \to \mathbb{T}$, and then we have
\begin{equation}\label{pde}
    \partial_{\alpha_1} \dots \partial_{\alpha_{|F_1|}} \tilde \Phi_{1} =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} 0
\end{equation} 
for all $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{|F_1|} \in \mathbb{T}$.  We claim that this implies that $\tilde \Phi_1$ is a linear function\footnote{See also \cite{Austin} for an extensive study on factorization of solutions to partial difference equations  in compact abelian groups (such as \eqref{pde}).}
\begin{equation}\label{nth}
\tilde \Phi_1(x) = n_1x + \theta_1 
\end{equation}
for some integer $n_1$ and $\theta_1 \in \mathbb{T}$, and almost all $x \in \mathbb{T}$.  We prove this by induction on the number $|F_1|$ of derivatives.  For $|F_1| \leq 1$, $\tilde \Phi_{1}$ is necessarily constant almost everywhere and the claim follows.  If $|F_1| > 1$, then by induction hypothesis, we see that for every $\alpha \in \mathbb{T}$ there exists an integer $n_\alpha$ and $\theta_\alpha \in \mathbb{T}$ such that
$$ \partial_\alpha \tilde \Phi_{1}(x) = n_\alpha x + \theta_\alpha$$
for almost every $x \in \mathbb{T}$.  As $\alpha \to 0$, the continuity of translation in the strong operator topology shows that $e^{2\pi i  \partial_\alpha \tilde \Phi_{1}}$ converges in $L^2(\mathbb{T})$ to the constant $1$, and hence $n_\alpha$ must vanish for $\alpha$ sufficiently close to the origin.  Using the cocycle identity
$$ \partial_{\alpha+\beta} \tilde \Phi_{1}(x) = 
 \partial_{\alpha} \tilde \Phi_{1}(x) +  \partial_{\beta} \tilde \Phi_{1}(x-\alpha)$$
 and induction we conclude that $n_\alpha$ vanishes for all $\alpha$.  This argument also shows that the map $\alpha \mapsto \theta_\alpha$ is a continuous homomorphism from $\mathbb{T}$ to $\mathbb{T}$, and is thus of the form $\theta_\alpha = n_1\alpha$ for some integer $n_1$.  The function $\tilde \Phi_{1}(x) - n_1x$ is then almost everywhere constant (since all of its derivatives vanish almost everywhere), and the claim follows.  In particular we have
\begin{equation}\label{phi-f1}
\Phi_{1}(x) = n_1 h_{f_1} \cdot x + \theta_1 \hbox{ mod } 1
\end{equation}
for almost all $x \in \mathbb{T}^2$.
  
Now suppose for contradiction that $h_{f_2} \neq \pm h_{f_1}$.  If we set
$$ \Phi_{2} \coloneqq \sum_{f \in F \backslash \mathbb{Q}^2: h_f = \pm h_{f_2}} \varphi_f$$
then by repeating the previous arguments, we can find an integer $n_2$ and $\theta_2 \in \mathbb{T}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{phi-f2}
\Phi_{2}(x) = n_2 h_{f_2} \cdot x + \theta_2 \hbox{ mod } 1
\end{equation}
for almost all $x \in \mathbb{T}^2$.

On the other hand, from \eqref{onet2} we have 
$$ \Phi_{1}(x) + \Phi_{2}(x) \leq 1 $$
for almost all $x \in \mathbb{T}^2$.  Since $\Phi_{1}$ is $\langle h_{f_1} \rangle^\perp$-invariant, and $\Phi_{2}$ is $\langle h_{f_2} \rangle^\perp$-invariant, and every coset of
$\langle h_{f_1} \rangle^\perp$ intersects every coset of $\langle h_{f_2} \rangle^\perp$, we have
$$ \| \Phi_{1} \|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^2)} + \| \Phi_{2} \|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^2)} = \| \Phi_{1} + \Phi_{2} \|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^2)}  \leq 1.$$
We conclude that for some $i=1,2$ we have
$$ \| \Phi_{i} \|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{T}^2)} \leq 1/2.$$
Comparing this with \eqref{phi-f1} or \eqref{phi-f2} we conclude that $n_i$ must vanish, and $\Phi_{i}$ is equal almost everywhere to a constant $c_i$.  Since $\Phi_{i} \geq \varphi_{f_i}$ and $\varphi_{f_i}$ has mean $1/|F|$, we have $c_i \geq 1/|F|$. From \eqref{onet2} we then have the inequality
$$ {\bf 1}_{\mathbb{T}^2} \geq {\bf 1}_A + 1/|F|$$
almost everywhere, but this contradicts the positive measure of $A$.  Hence $h_{f_1} = \pm h_{f_2}$ as required.

title: Remark
body_md:
Suppose that $F \oplus A =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^d$ is a measurable tiling of the $d$-torus, $d\geq 2$, by some finite subset $F = \{f_1,\dots,f_n\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ and some measurable subset $A$ of $\mathbb{T}^d$. Consider the velocities $v_i$ as in \cref{thm:torus}(i), and let  $F_{(v)} \coloneqq \{ f_i: v_i = v \}$ be  those elements of $F$ that are moving with velocity $v$.  \cref{thm:torus}(ii) gives that the sets $F_{(v)} \oplus A$ are $\mathbb{R} v$-invariant for every $v \in \mathbb{R}^2$.
In dimensions $d\ge 3$ this is no longer true. For instance, if $A=[0,1/2]^3$ and 
\begin{align*}
     F = \{ 
     &(0,0,0), (0,1/2,0),\\
     &(1/2, 0, 0), (1/2, 1/2, 0)\\
     &(\alpha,0 , 1/2), (\alpha,1/2, 1/2),\\
     &(\alpha+1/2, \beta, 1/2), (\alpha+1/2, \beta+1/2, 1/2)
     \}
\end{align*} for some irrationally numbers $\alpha,\beta$, and $F^0=\{0,1/2\}^3$. Then, if $v=(\alpha, \beta)$ or $v=(\alpha,0)$, we have that $F_{(v)}\oplus A$ is not $\mathbb{R} v$-invariant.

However, we do not know if there is any measurable tiling $F\oplus A=_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^d$, $d\ge 3$ that does not satisfy the following weaker analogue of \cref{thm:torus}(ii).
The velocities are replaced with piecewise linear functions $v_f:[0,1]\to \mathbb{R}^d$, for $f\in F$, such that $F^t\oplus A=_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^d$, where $F^t$ is defined analogously as in \cref{thm:torus}.
Moreover, if we set $F^t_{(v)}=\{f\in F:v'_f(t)=v\}$, for $v\in \mathbb{R}^d$, then $F^t_{(v)}\oplus A$ is $\mathbb{R} v$-invariant for every $v\in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $t\in [0,1]$ whenever all the derivatives exist.
In fact, we do not even know whether there exists any measurable tiling $F\oplus A=_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^d$, $d\ge 3$ such that there is no velocity $0\not= v\in \mathbb{R}^d$ for which there is a proper non-empty subset $F'$ of $F$ such that $F'\oplus A$ is $\mathbb{R} v$-invariant.
Note that the argument in \cite{Szabo} implies that if the tile $A$ is a cube then every tiling $F$ satisfies this weaker analogue of \cref{thm:torus}(ii).
On the other hand, if we are allowed to use more than one tile, then we  can construct such a tiling in $\mathbb{T}^3$, as follows.  Let $f \colon \mathbb{T} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the function
$$ f(x) \coloneqq \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{10}$$ 
and consider the following subsets $A_1, A_2, A_3$ of $\mathbb{T}^3$:
\begin{align*}
     A_1 &\coloneqq \{ (x,y,z \hbox{ mod 1}): (x,y) \in {\mathbb{T}}^2: f(x) \leq z < 1/3 + f(x+y) \}\\
 A_2 &\coloneqq \{ (x,y,z \hbox{ mod 1}): (x,y) \in {\mathbb{T}}^2: 1/3+f(x+y) \leq z < 2/3 + f(y) \}\\
 A_3 &\coloneqq \{ (x,y,z \hbox{ mod 1}): (x,y) \in {\mathbb{T}}^2: 2/3+f(y) \leq z < 1 + f(x) \}.
\end{align*}
It is a routine matter to verify that
$$ ((t,0,0) + A_1) \uplus ((0,t,0) + A_2) \uplus ((t,t,0) + A_3) =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^3$$ 
for any $t \in \mathbb{R}$, but that none of the individual sets $A_1, A_2, A_3$ enjoy any translational symmetries.  Thus we see that there is a non-rigidity to the tiling problem
$$ (f_1+A_1) \uplus (f_2 + A_2) \uplus (f_3 + A_3) =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^3$$
that cannot be explained purely by sliding each of the $A_1,A_2,A_3$ separately, or by translating the entire triple $A_1,A_2,A_3$ by a common shift.

name: Connected tilings of intervals

label: one-eq
title: Proof
body_md:
By translation and rescaling, we may normalize $[a,b] = [0,1]$ to be the unit interval, and also normalize $\min F = 0$.  
We enumerate the distinct elements of $F$ in order as 
$$0 = f_1<f_2<\dots<f_k$$ 
and write $${\bf 1}_F=\sum_{j=1}^k m_{j}{\bf 1}_{\{f_j\}},$$ where $m_{j} \geq 1$ is the multiplicity of $f_j$ in $F$; thus
\begin{equation}\label{one-eq}
 {\bf 1}_{[0,1]}(x) = \sum_{j=1}^k m_j \psi(x - f_j)
 \end{equation}
for almost every $x$. 

If $k=1$ then the claim immediately follows from \eqref{one-eq}.  Henceforth we assume $k > 1$.  Let $[c,c']$ be the support of $\psi$, then the support of $\sum_{j=1}^k m_j \psi(x - f_j)$ has infimum $c$ and supremum $f_k+c'$, thus by \eqref{one-eq} we have $c'>c=0$ and 
\begin{equation}\label{fk-range}
0 < f_k = 1-c' < 1.
\end{equation}

From \eqref{one-eq}, focusing attention in particular on the $j=1$ term on the right-hand side, we have
\begin{equation}\label{c1}
 1 \geq m_{1} \psi(x)
\end{equation}
for almost every $0 \leq x \leq 1$, with equality for almost every $0 \leq x \leq f_2$.  Focusing instead on the $j=k$ term, we have
\begin{equation}\label{ck}
 1 \geq m_k \psi(x-f_k)
\end{equation}
for almost every $0 \leq x \leq 1$, with equality for almost every $f_{k-1}+c' \leq x \leq 1$.  Combining these facts, we see that for almost every $f_k \leq x \leq \min(1, f_k+f_2)$ we have
$$ 1 \geq m_k \psi(x-f_k) = \frac{m_k}{m_1}$$
and for almost every $\max(0, f_{k-1}-f_k+c') \leq x \leq c'$ we have
$$ 1 \geq m_1 \psi(x) = \frac{m_1}{m_k}.$$
Since both of these ranges of $x$ have positive measure, we have $m_1=m_k=m$ for some natural number $m$, and
$$ \psi(x) = \frac{1}{m}$$
for almost every $0 \leq x \leq \delta \coloneqq \min(1,f_k+f_2)-f_k$.  Returning to \eqref{one-eq}, and isolating the $j=k$ term again, we see that
$$ 1 = 1 + \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} m_j \psi(x-f_j)$$
for almost all $f_k \leq x \leq \min(f_k+\delta,1)$.  In particular we have $\psi(x) = 0$ for almost all $f_k-f_{k-1} \leq x \leq \min(f_k+\delta,1) - f_{k-1}$.  Since $\psi$ is supported on $[0,c']$, this implies that $c' \leq f_k - f_{k-1}$.  Thus the functions $\psi(x-f_j)$ vanish for all $1 \leq j \leq k-1$ and almost all $x \geq f_k \geq f_j+c'$; inserting this back into \eqref{one-eq} we conclude that
$$ {\bf 1}_{[0,1]}(x) = m \psi(x-f_k)$$
for almost all $x \geq f_k$.  Thus $m \psi =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} {\bf 1}_{[0,1-f_k]}= {\bf 1}_{[c,c']}$, and the claim follows.

title: Remark
body_md:
The hypothesis that $A$ is open and connected can be relaxed to the hypothesis that $A$ is ``measurably connected'' in the following sense: for every $\xi \in \mathbb{Z}^2 \backslash \{0\}$, the function $\psi_\xi \colon \mathbb{T} \to [0,+\infty)$ defined by
$$ \psi_\xi(t) \coloneqq \int_{\xi \cdot x = t} {\bf 1}_A,$$
where the integral is with respect to the Haar probability measure on $\{ x \in \mathbb{T}^2: \xi \cdot x=t\}$, has connected support (modulo null sets).  We leave the details of this generalization to the interested reader.

title: Remark
body_md:
The \emph{periodic tiling conjecture} \cite{GS-book, Lagarias-Wang} asserts that if one has a tiling $F \oplus A = \mathbb{Z}^d$ for some finite tile $F$ in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and $A\subset \mathbb{Z}^d$, then there is also a periodic tiling $F \oplus A' = \mathbb{Z}^d$, thus $A'$ is a finite union of cosets of some lattice in $\mathbb{Z}^d$.  Currently this conjecture has only been established up to $d \leq 2$; see \cite{bhattacharya2020periodicity,GreenfeldTao}.  A variant of the argument used to prove \cref{thm:torus}(i) can establish the following partial result towards this conjecture: suppose that there is a homomorphism $T \colon \mathbb{Z}^d \to \mathbb{T}^m$ and a measurable subset $E$ of the torus $\mathbb{T}^m$ and a finite $F\subset \mathbb{Z}^d$ such that one has the measurable tiling $T(F) \oplus E =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^m$, where an element $f$ of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ acts on $\mathbb{T}^m$ via translation by $T(f)$.  Then $F$ admits a periodic tiling $F \oplus A' = \mathbb{Z}^d$.  Indeed, if one defines ${\mathcal T}(F)$ to be the space of homomorphisms $\tilde T \colon \mathbb{Z}^d \to \mathbb{T}^m$ (which one can identify with $(\mathbb{T}^m)^d$) such that $\tilde T(F) \oplus E =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^m$, then a variant of the above arguments shows that ${\mathcal T}(F)$ contains the orbit closure
$$ \overline{ \{ (nq+1) T: n \in \mathbb{Z} \} }.$$
By the above analysis, this orbit closure contains a rational point $T^0$, and by restricting the measurable tiling $T^0(F) \oplus E =_{\mathrm{a.e.}} \mathbb{T}^m$ to a generic coset of $T^0(\mathbb{Z}^d)$ and pulling back by $\mathbb{Z}^d$ one obtains a periodic tiling $F \oplus A' = \mathbb{Z}^d$; we leave the details to the interested reader.

label: existenceMean
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{existenceMean} \cite[Section 3]{CieslaSabok-Hall}
Let $\nu$ be a Borel probability measure on $[0,1]^{\mathbb{N}}$.
Then there is a medial mean 
$$\operatorname{m} \colon \ell_\infty\to \mathbb{R}$$
that is $\nu$-measurable when restricted to $[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ (i.e., it is measurable with respect to the completion of the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ by $\nu$).

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\gamma(N)=\alpha(N)-\beta(N)$.
It is enough to show that $\operatorname{m}(\gamma)=0$.
We have $-|\gamma|\le \gamma\le |\gamma|$.
By positivity and additivity of $\operatorname{m}$ this gives $\operatorname{m}(|\gamma|)\ge \operatorname{m}(\gamma)\ge -\operatorname{m}(|\gamma|)$, as we have
$$\operatorname{m}(|\gamma|)-\operatorname{m}(\gamma)=\operatorname{m}(|\gamma|-\gamma)\ge 0$$
and similarly
$$\operatorname{m}(\gamma)-\operatorname{m}(-|\gamma|)=\operatorname{m}(\gamma-(-|\gamma|))\ge 0.$$
Consequently, it is enough to show that $\operatorname{m}(|\gamma|)=0$.
We have
$$\operatorname{m}(|\gamma|)=\operatorname{m}(S^k |\gamma|)\le \operatorname{m}(\max S^k |\gamma|)=\max S^k |\gamma|\to 0$$
by shift-invariance, normality and positivity.
